title: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
summary: From blue boxes and the Morris worm to SolarWinds and xz: what happened in each landmark incident, why it worked, what it cost, and the laws, institutions and safer defaults it left behind.
outcomes: Explain the mechanism and root pattern behind landmark incidents from 1960 to 2024
Explain why in-band control, unpatched services, trusted perimeters and trusted suppliers keep recurring
Compute how doubling time decides whether people can respond to a worm
Trace how each incident led to a change in law, institutions, defaults or architecture
Read an incident report and answer what happened, why it worked, what it cost and what changed
Choose the defences that fit a new incident by matching it to its historical pattern

lessons.title: Why old attacks still matter: five eras, five patterns

blocks.md:
Why spend time on a whistle from the 1960s or a worm from 1988? Because the same few mistakes keep coming back with new technology, and the fixes people built after each incident are the defaults you now take for granted: a firewall that is on when Windows installs, email that refuses to open a script, a national team you can report a bug to.

A tiny example. In 1960 a student noticed that the phone network let a caller's sound act as a command to the network. In 2021 a logging library let text inside a log message act as a command to the server. Sixty years apart, the bug has the same shape: **data that the system treats as control**.

This course retells landmark **incidents** (events that actually or potentially harmed the confidentiality, integrity or availability of a system, the CIA triad from *Security from zero*). For each one you will learn four things: **what happened**, **why it worked**, **what it cost**, and **what changed afterwards** in law, institutions or engineering.

Two words recur. NIST's glossary defines a [**worm**](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/worm) as a self-contained program that can propagate itself through computer networks, and a [**virus**](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/virus) as malicious software that spreads by modifying other programs or files to include a copy of itself, running when the infected program is opened. So a virus needs a person to open something; a worm does not.

Everything here is told at the level of court records, government reports and journalism. Exploit details stay out: the point is the mechanism and the lesson.

blocks.title: Five eras of incidents (axis: years after 1955)

scenes.caption: 1960 to 1976: phone phreaks control long-distance switches with tones, until the network moves its signalling onto a separate channel (lesson 2).
1986 to 1995: a 75-cent accounting gap exposes a spy, the Morris worm crashes the research internet, and Kevin Mitnick shows how far phone calls and lies can go (lessons 3 and 4).
1999 to 2008: email viruses and self-spreading worms hit millions of ordinary PCs. Vendors respond with blocked attachments, firewalls on by default and automatic updates (lessons 5 to 7).
2010 to 2017: state operations become public (Aurora, Stuxnet, NotPetya) and breaches reach tens of millions of records (Target, OPM) (lessons 8 to 11).
2020 to 2024: attackers go through the software people trust and install: a signed update, a logging library, a file-transfer product, a compression library (lessons 12 and 13).

blocks.md:
Across the eras, five root patterns explain most of the incidents in this course:

1. **Control mixed with data**: the system lets input act as an instruction (blue boxes, Log4Shell).
2. **A known flaw left open**: a patch existed but was not installed, or a risky feature was left switched on (the Morris worm's sendmail debug mode, Code Red, Slammer, Conficker, WannaCry).
3. **People tricked**: someone is persuaded to reveal a secret or open a file (Mitnick, ILOVEYOU).
4. **A trusted perimeter**: once inside the network, an intruder is trusted (Aurora, Target, OPM).
5. **A trusted supplier**: the attack arrives through software or a company you rely on (NotPetya, SolarWinds, xz).

The short script below is how this course will keep score. It tags each incident with its main pattern.

blocks.code:
from collections import Counter

# (incident, year, root pattern) as told in this course
incidents = [
    ("Blue boxes", 1960, "control mixed with data"),
    ("Morris worm", 1988, "known flaw left open"),
    ("Mitnick", 1995, "people tricked"),
    ("ILOVEYOU", 2000, "people tricked"),
    ("Code Red", 2001, "known flaw left open"),
    ("Slammer", 2003, "known flaw left open"),
    ("Conficker", 2008, "known flaw left open"),
    ("Aurora", 2010, "trusted perimeter"),
    ("Target", 2013, "trusted perimeter"),
    ("OPM", 2015, "trusted perimeter"),
    ("NotPetya", 2017, "trusted supplier"),
    ("SolarWinds", 2020, "trusted supplier"),
    ("Log4Shell", 2021, "control mixed with data"),
    ("xz-utils", 2024, "trusted supplier"),
]
for pattern, n in Counter(p for _, _, p in incidents).most_common():
    years = [y for _, y, p in incidents if p == pattern]
    print(f"{pattern:28} {n}  first {min(years)}, latest {max(years)}")

# Output:
# known flaw left open         4  first 1988, latest 2008
# trusted perimeter            3  first 2010, latest 2015
# trusted supplier             3  first 2017, latest 2024
# control mixed with data      2  first 1960, latest 2021
# people tricked               2  first 1995, latest 2000
blocks.caption: Real output. The tags are this course's simplification: most incidents mix several patterns (the Morris worm also guessed passwords; NotPetya also used a leaked exploit).

blocks.md: Hindsight makes every incident look obvious. At the time, the engineers involved were usually competent people working with the knowledge and trade-offs of their day. Read each case asking "what would have had to be true for this to be caught?", not "how could they be so careless?"

Each incident in this course is told the same way: what happened, why it worked (which pattern), what it cost, and what changed. The changes are the useful part: they are the controls you will be asked to run and defend.

blocks.question: A 2021 bug let text written into a log message be treated as an instruction by the logging library. Which 1960s problem has the same root pattern?
options: Phone phreaks guessing operator passwords
Mainframe users sharing accounts
Blue boxes: a caller's tone on the voice line was taken as a command by the switch
Stolen magnetic-stripe cards
blocks.explain: Both let data travelling on the normal channel (a sound on the voice line, text in a log message) act as control. The other options are real problems but different patterns: weak secrets, shared accounts and physical theft.

lessons.title: Phone phreaking: when the voice line was also the control line

blocks.md:
In the 1950s and 1960s AT&T, the US telephone monopoly (nicknamed Ma Bell), ran the long-distance network with automatic switching machines in each city. Phil Lapsley, a historian of phone hacking, explains in IEEE Spectrum how they talked to each other: **with tones on the same line that carried your voice**. On an idle trunk (a long-distance line between two switches), each end sent a steady **2600 Hz** tone meaning "this line is free". When a call started the tone stopped, and the dialled digits were sent as more tones.

Sending control signals inside the voice channel is called **in-band signalling** (the "band" is the range of audio frequencies the call uses). Its weakness: anything that can make a sound on the line can speak the network's control language.

**Phreaking** (Wikipedia: a sensational spelling of *freak* with the *ph* of *phone*) was the culture of people who explored the phone network this way. Lapsley tells of Ralph Barclay, an 18-year-old first-year student at Washington State University, who in late 1960 found an article in the November 1960 *Bell System Technical Journal*, "Signaling Systems for Control of Telephone Switching". It listed the frequencies the switches used. In Lapsley's account Barclay's key insight was that a 2600 Hz tone sent by the caller reset the **far** switch but not the local one, and the local switch did the billing. Barclay built tone generators; a later, improved one was housed in a metal box that happened to be painted blue, which is where the name **blue box** comes from.

The engineers who published the article had not seen the flaw. As Lapsley puts it, once the hole is explained it looks obvious.

scenes.caption: Idle trunk: each switch sends 2600 Hz to the other, meaning 'this line is free'. The tone travels on the same path voices use.
A normal call to a free number: the local switch seizes the trunk, sends the digits as tones, and starts billing for that free call.
The flaw: a tone the caller plays into the mouthpiece reaches the far switch, which cannot tell it from a switch's own signal and treats the trunk as free for new instructions.
The fix (CCIS, from 1976): switches signal over a separate data link that callers cannot reach. Sounds on the voice line are only sounds.

blocks.title: Toy switch: in-band versus out-of-band control
blocks.code:
# Toy model of a trunk switch. Not real telephony: one string per sound.
def in_band_switch(line_sounds):
    state = "call to free number"
    for sound in line_sounds:            # control and voice share the line
        if sound == "2600Hz":
            state = "trunk idle, ready for new digits"
        elif state.startswith("trunk idle"):
            state = "routed to " + sound
    return state

def out_of_band_switch(line_sounds, signalling_link):
    state = "call to free number"
    for msg in signalling_link:          # only the switches can write here
        state = msg
    return state                         # line_sounds are just audio

caller = ["hello", "2600Hz", "any-number"]
print(in_band_switch(caller))
print(out_of_band_switch(caller, ["call to free number"]))

scenes.caption: The caller's line carries three sounds. In the in-band switch, every sound is inspected for control meaning.
The first sound is speech; the state stays 'call to free number', which is what billing sees.
The caller's 2600Hz matches the control token, so the switch resets the trunk. Data has become control.

vars.state: trunk idle, ready for new digits

scenes.caption: The next sound is taken as routing digits.
The out-of-band switch only reads its signalling link, which callers cannot write to. The same sounds change nothing.
scenes.output:
routed to any-number
call to free number

blocks.md: **Captain Crunch and the Esquire story.** Phreaks discovered that a toy whistle given away in boxes of Cap'n Crunch cereal (in 1963, according to [Draper's Wikipedia biography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Draper)) produced a 2600 Hz tone. John Draper learned of it and took the nickname Captain Crunch. In October 1971 *Esquire* published Ron Rosenbaum's "Secrets of the Little Blue Box", built largely on interviews with Draper. According to the same biography, the article's notoriety led to Draper's arrest by the FBI in May 1972 on wire fraud charges, and the article led Steve Wozniak, then an engineering student at UC Berkeley, to seek Draper out, bringing a friend, Steve Jobs.

**What changed.** The real fix was architectural. Bell Labs records that in May 1976 a new **Common Channel Interoffice Signaling** (CCIS) system linked a toll office in Madison, Wisconsin to one in Chicago: control messages moved to a separate high-speed data channel shared by many trunks (hence *common channel*: one signalling channel controls many voice channels, as [Wikipedia's article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common-channel_signaling) puts it). Users had no path into it. The conversion took years: Wikipedia's [history of the blue box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_box) notes that by the 1980s switches with separate signalling served almost all major exchanges, leaving only corners of the network open to the trick.

In-band signalling fails because whoever can send data can also send commands. The durable fix is to separate the control channel from the data channel so the attacker has no way to reach it. You will meet the same idea as parameterised SQL queries and as never evaluating text found inside log messages.

Filtering out the 2600 Hz tone would have been a weak fix: phreaks used many other tones, and a filter on a shared channel is always a race. Removing the attacker's access to the control channel ended the whole class of trick.

blocks.question: Why did a 2600 Hz tone from a caller fool the far switch?
options: The switch could not tell a caller's tone from another switch's control tone, because both arrived on the same voice path
The tone carried a password the switch accepted
The tone overloaded the switch's power supply
The local switch forwarded it as a data packet
blocks.explain: In-band signalling means the control language travels in the same audio band as voices. Nothing marked a tone as coming from a switch rather than a person, so the far switch obeyed it.

blocks.question: Which change ended blue boxing as a class of attack?
options: Arresting John Draper in 1972
Publishing fewer technical journals
Adding a louder 2600 Hz tone
Moving inter-switch signalling to a separate channel (CCIS) that callers could not reach
blocks.explain: Arrests and secrecy did not remove the mechanism; plenty of people knew the frequencies. Out-of-band signalling removed the attacker's access to the control channel entirely.

lessons.title: A 75-cent gap and the Morris worm: the 1980s internet learns

blocks.md:
By the 1980s, universities and laboratories were connected by networks that later merged into the internet. Users were mostly researchers who knew each other, and security relied on that trust.

**The Cuckoo's Egg, 1986.** Clifford Stoll, an astronomer running computers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) in California, was asked to explain a 75-cent discrepancy in the lab's computer-usage accounting. The lab charged scientists for computer time, and two records of usage did not agree. As told in Stoll's 1989 book *The Cuckoo's Egg* (summarised by [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cuckoo%27s_Egg_%28book%29) and by Red Hat's *Command Line Heroes* podcast), the gap traced to an account with no billing owner, which led to an intruder. Over months Stoll logged the intruder's sessions, and with the FBI, other US agencies and the West German post office (which ran the phone system there) traced the calls to Markus Hess in Hanover, who was selling what Hess found to the Soviet KGB (Committee for State Security, the USSR's main intelligence and security agency).

Two lessons from Stoll's hunt still define detection work. First, **reconcile records that should agree**: a small mismatch between two independent logs is a signal, not rounding noise. Second, **a decoy can make an intruder reveal themselves**: Stoll created a fictitious project account full of convincing but fake documents (the book's "SDInet"), which Wikipedia notes is known today as a **honeypot** (a system or file that has no legitimate users, so any use of it is suspicious).

Here is the reconciliation idea as code. The accounts and amounts are made up; the shape of the check is the point.

blocks.code:
# Toy reconciliation: two records of the same computer use should agree.
# Amounts in cents; account names and numbers are made up.
system_log = {"alice": 1250, "bob": 830, "chen": 2115, "hunter": 75}
billing    = {"alice": 1250, "bob": 830, "chen": 2115}   # paying accounts only

gap = sum(system_log.values()) - sum(billing.values())
print("unbilled cents:", gap)
for user, cents in system_log.items():
    if user not in billing:
        print("no billing record for account:", user, cents, "cents")

# Output:
# unbilled cents: 75
# no billing record for account: hunter 75 cents
blocks.caption: Real output. The same pattern finds intruders today: compare VPN logins against the HR list of staff, or cloud API usage against what the billing team expects.

blocks.md:
**The Morris worm, 2 November 1988.** You met this case in *Security from zero*: a program written by graduate student Robert T. Morris spread through four doors (a sendmail debug feature, a buffer overflow in the `fingerd` service, trusted-host files and password guessing), and Morris was convicted under the then-new US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

Why did a program meant to spread quietly bring machines to a halt? Donn Seeley's analysis, *A Tour of the Worm*, describes a "population control" step: when a worm found another copy on the same machine, the two were supposed to negotiate so that one would exit. But a test at the top of that routine made 1 in 7 copies skip the negotiation and become, in Seeley's word, immortal. Reinfections kept adding copies, each consuming processor time.

blocks.title: Copies on one machine after repeated reinfection (simplified)

scenes.caption: If population control always worked, every new arrival would negotiate with the resident copy and one would exit: one copy per machine, whatever the arrivals.
With 1 in 7 arrivals skipping the negotiation, the expected count is 1 + arrivals/7: 2 after 7, 3 after 14, 6 after 35, 11 after 70. Simplified: the real worm's rules had more cases.

blocks.md:
**What changed after Morris.**

- **A coordination centre.** The Software Engineering Institute (SEI) at Carnegie Mellon University records that, in the aftermath of the worm, DARPA (the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency) asked it to set up a computer emergency response team, which became the **CERT Coordination Center** (CERT/CC; CERT originally stood for Computer Emergency Response Team). It acts as a neutral third party between vulnerability reporters and vendors, and it helped build a network of more than 50 national incident response teams.
- **Shared response.** RFC 1135, a 1989 retrospective, says the Berkeley and MIT teams exchanged code and fixes over informal networks of system administrators and that the worm was eliminated from most computers within 48 to 72 hours.
- **Law in use.** The conviction showed that the 1986 computer crime law applied to self-spreading code.

blocks.prompt: A defender sees processor load climb on a machine that has already been cleaned once. Using the 1-in-7 rule, why might cleaning one machine at a time never win while its neighbours stay infected?
blocks.reveal: Because reinfection keeps arriving from neighbours. Each arrival has a chance of leaving an extra immortal copy, so the count on an exposed machine grows with time. RFC 1135 records that once sites patched the sendmail and fingerd holes the worm was stopped and could not reinfect them: removing the way in, not killing processes, is what stops reinfection.

blocks.md: 1980s lessons that still hold: reconcile records that should agree; plant decoys that only an intruder would touch; and when something spreads, close the entry points rather than chasing copies. The worm also produced an institution, CERT/CC, which is why there is now a neutral place to report vulnerabilities.

blocks.question: Why was a 75-cent accounting difference worth investigating?
options: 75 cents was a large sum of money in 1986
Two independent records of the same activity disagreed, and the difference came from an account with no legitimate owner
Billing systems never make rounding errors
Stoll suspected the KGB from the start
blocks.explain: The value of the gap did not matter; the disagreement between two records that should match did. The unbilled account was the intruder's. Stoll did not know who was behind it until months later.

blocks.question: What made the Morris worm overload machines it had already infected?
options: It encrypted their disks
Its population control let 1 in 7 copies skip the check that should make duplicates exit, so reinfections piled up copies
It deliberately deleted system files
It sent large amounts of email spam
blocks.explain: Seeley's analysis: a test made 1 in 7 worms skip population control and become immortal. Repeated reinfection therefore multiplied processes. The worm did not encrypt or delete files.

lessons.title: Kevin Mitnick: social engineering and the longest sentence of its day

blocks.md:
Kevin Mitnick was the most famous intruder of the early 1990s. The clearest record is the US Department of Justice press release of 9 August 1999, which announced Mitnick's sentence of 46 months in federal prison after a plea agreement.

**What happened**, in the government's words: Mitnick pleaded guilty to four counts of wire fraud, two counts of computer fraud and one count of illegally intercepting a wire communication, for a 2.5-year hacking spree that ended with an arrest in North Carolina in February 1995. Mitnick admitted breaking into computer systems and stealing proprietary software belonging to Motorola, Novell, Fujitsu, Sun Microsystems and other companies, and impersonating employees of victim companies, including Nokia Mobile Phones, to try to obtain software under development.

**Why it worked.** The release lists the tools Mitnick admitted using: **social engineering**, cloned cellular telephones, **sniffer** programs placed on victims' computers, and hacker software. Social engineering is manipulating people into giving access or information, for example by phoning as a colleague who needs a file; it works because staff are trained to be helpful and rarely trained to verify. A sniffer is a program that records network traffic passing a machine, which in that era often included passwords sent in clear text.

The common thread is **identity proven by assertion**: a voice on the phone saying "I'm from engineering" was believed. That is pattern 3 from lesson 1, people tricked.

blocks.title: A help-desk reset: believing the caller versus calling back

scenes.caption: The caller claims to be an employee and asks for a password reset, giving a phone number for the new password.
Vulnerable process: the help desk trusts the claim and delivers the new password to the number the caller supplied. The caller now owns the account.
Fixed process: the help desk ignores contact details given on the call and looks up the number already on file.
The call-back reaches the real employee, who did not ask for a reset. The request is refused and reported as an attempted impersonation.

blocks.code:
# Help-desk password reset. Directory data is made up.
DIRECTORY = {"j.ortiz": {"phone": "+1-555-0100", "manager": "k.lee"}}

def reset_vulnerable(user, caller_says_phone):
    # trusts whatever the caller says on this call
    return f"reset {user}, new password read out to {caller_says_phone}"

def reset_fixed(user, caller_says_phone):
    rec = DIRECTORY.get(user)
    if rec is None:
        return "refuse: unknown user"
    # never use contact details supplied by the caller: call back the
    # number already on file and notify the manager out of band
    return (f"call back {rec['phone']} (on file, ignoring {caller_says_phone}); "
            f"notify {rec['manager']}; reset only after callback answers")

print(reset_vulnerable("j.ortiz", "+1-555-0199"))
print(reset_fixed("j.ortiz", "+1-555-0199"))

# Output:
# reset j.ortiz, new password read out to +1-555-0199
# call back +1-555-0100 (on file, ignoring +1-555-0199); notify k.lee; reset only after callback answers
blocks.caption: Real output. Why the fix works: the attacker controls everything said on the call, but not the directory or the real employee's phone. Verification goes through a channel the caller cannot reach, the same idea as out-of-band signalling.

blocks.md:
**What it cost, and what the court did.** The release says victims reported millions of dollars in losses (lost licensing fees, delays, research and repairs), but Judge Mariana Pfaelzer ordered restitution of only about USD 4,125, citing Mitnick's limited future earnings. With an earlier 22-month term for cloned phones and supervised-release violations, the combined 68 months was described as the longest sentence given to any computer hacker at that time. On release, three years of supervised release would severely restrict Mitnick's access to computers and work in the computer industry.

**What changed.** The case put social engineering into security vocabulary and training. Help-desk call-back rules, verification questions that do not rely on publicly known facts, and logging of every reset are its direct descendants. The modern version of the same attack is the caller who persuades a help desk to reset multi-factor authentication; the course *Phishing, social engineering and email security* covers it in depth.

"We'll train staff not to be fooled" is a weak defence on its own: a skilled caller is persuasive and polite, and the help desk is measured on speed. Build the process so that even a fooled agent cannot complete a reset without the out-of-band check.

Social engineering attacks the process, not the person. The fix is a process in which identity is proven through a channel the requester does not control (call-back to a number on file, manager approval, in-person check), and every reset is logged and reviewed.

blocks.question: A caller passes three knowledge questions (date of birth, manager's name, office location) and asks for a reset. Why is this still weak verification?
options: These facts can often be found or guessed by an outsider, so they prove little; a call-back to a number on file does not depend on what the caller knows
Knowledge questions are always encrypted
Three questions are too many and annoy staff
Managers' names are secret by law
blocks.explain: Birthdays, managers and offices often appear on social media or company sites. Proof should come from something the attacker cannot supply on the call, such as the real employee answering the phone number already on file.

blocks.question: According to the 1999 Justice Department release, which of these did Mitnick NOT list among the tools used?
options: Social engineering
Cloned cellular telephones
A self-spreading worm
Sniffer programs
blocks.explain: The plea listed social engineering, cloned cell phones, sniffers and hacker software. Mitnick's intrusions were targeted and hands-on; nothing in the plea describes self-spreading code.

lessons.title: Melissa and ILOVEYOU: viruses that used your address book

blocks.md:
By the late 1990s millions of office PCs ran Microsoft Word and the Outlook email program. Both could run small programs: **macros** in Word (scripts embedded in a document to automate tasks) and **VBScript** files (Visual Basic Scripting Edition) through the Windows Script Host (WSH, the Windows component that runs script files). Outlook also let programs read the address book and send mail. Put together, a document or attachment could mail itself to everyone you know.

**Melissa, 26 March 1999.** The US Attorney's release on the sentencing of its author, David L. Smith, explains: Smith posted an infected Word document to an internet newsgroup, enticing readers to open it. Once opened, the virus lowered Word's macro security settings, infected documents, and, on computers using Outlook, sent an infected email to the first 50 addresses in the user's address book, with the message "Here is that document you asked for ... don't show anyone else;-)".

Melissa spread so fast because each infection fanned out to 50 more mailboxes, from a sender the recipient knew. Smith acknowledged in a plea agreement that it caused more than USD 80 million in damage, mostly by overloading email servers until networks were shut down. Smith was arrested on 1 April 1999 after a tip from America Online and in May 2002 was sentenced to 20 months in federal prison.

The plot shows the arithmetic of a fan-out of 50, ignoring overlap between address books (real spread was smaller because many people share contacts, but still fast).

blocks.title: Mailboxes reached per generation with fan-out f (simplified)

curves.label: f to the power of generation

scenes.caption: Melissa's fan-out of 50: 50 mailboxes after one generation, 2,500 after two, 125,000 after three (if every recipient opened it and nobody overlapped).
With a fan-out of 10, three generations reach 1,000. Throttling how many messages a program may send is one way to slow a mailer.
With a fan-out of 2, three generations reach only 8. Limits on automatic sending turn an explosion into a trickle that people can notice.

blocks.md:
**ILOVEYOU (the Love Letter worm), 4 May 2000.** CERT/CC's advisory CA-2000-04 describes a VBScript program arriving as an attachment named `LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU.TXT.VBS`, subject "ILOVEYOU", body "kindly check the attached LOVELETTER coming from me." When run, it mailed itself through Outlook to every entry in every address book, overwrote files such as `.jpg` and `.js` with copies of itself, and spread over IRC (Internet Relay Chat) and shared drives. By 8 May CERT/CC had reports from more than 650 sites covering more than 500,000 affected systems.

**Why it worked.** With Windows' "Hide extensions for known file types" setting, many people saw only `LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU.TXT` and assumed a harmless text file; the real extension, `.VBS`, meant "run this script". The message came from someone they knew. CERT/CC's advice included disabling Windows Script Host and filtering the attachment at the mail server.

blocks.code:
# Mail-gateway attachment check. Judge the LAST extension (the one Windows
# uses to decide what runs the file) against an allowlist.
ALLOWED = {"pdf", "txt", "jpg", "png", "docx", "xlsx"}

def verdict(filename):
    parts = filename.lower().split(".")
    last = parts[-1] if len(parts) > 1 else ""
    if last not in ALLOWED:
        return f"BLOCK (.{last} not allowed)"
    if len(parts) > 2:
        return "QUARANTINE (two extensions)"
    return "allow"

for name in ["report.txt", "LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU.TXT.vbs",
             "photo.jpg.vbs", "invoice.pdf.txt", "minutes.docx"]:
    print(f"{name:28} {verdict(name)}")

# Output:
# report.txt                   allow
# LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU.TXT.vbs  BLOCK (.vbs not allowed)
# photo.jpg.vbs                BLOCK (.vbs not allowed)
# invoice.pdf.txt              QUARANTINE (two extensions)
# minutes.docx                 allow
blocks.caption: Real output. The check reads the last extension, which is what decides how Windows opens a file, and uses an allowlist: a new dangerous type is blocked by default instead of waiting to be added to a blocklist.

blocks.md:
**What changed.**

- **Email clients stopped trusting attachments and programs.** A Microsoft Outlook tester, writing in a Microsoft blog about [the history of Outlook attachment security](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/blogs/kclemson/the-history-of-attachment-security-in-outlook-part-1-1), describes the response that followed ILOVEYOU: Outlook would simply refuse to open certain file types, would ask the user before a program could read addresses, and showed a dialog with a five-second wait before a program could send mail, so a script could not fire off hundreds of messages.
- **Law.** [Wikipedia's account of ILOVEYOU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ILOVEYOU) notes that its suspected author, in the Philippines, could not be prosecuted because no law covered the act; the Philippines passed the Electronic Commerce Act (Republic Act 8792) in June 2000, too late to apply retroactively.
- **Prosecution worked where law existed.** Melissa's author was convicted under the US computer fraud statute.

A blocklist of bad extensions (what the 2000 patch began with) needs constant updating and misses new types. Gateways today block by default and allow a short list of needed types, open documents in protected sandboxes, and Microsoft Office now [blocks macros in files from the internet](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365-apps/security/internet-macros-blocked) by default.

Mass mailers exploited trust in three things at once: the sender (a friend's address), the file (a hidden extension) and the program (Outlook let scripts read addresses and send mail). Each fix removed one trust: show real extensions, block executable attachments, and make programs ask before using your address book or sending.

blocks.question: Why did `LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU.TXT.VBS` fool so many people?
options: Its text was encrypted
It exploited a buffer overflow when previewed
It was digitally signed by Microsoft
Windows hid the real extension by default, so it looked like a .TXT file, and it came from a known contact
blocks.explain: Hidden extensions showed only LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU.TXT, and the sender was a friend whose machine was infected. Opening it ran a script; no memory-corruption bug was needed.

blocks.question: Melissa sent itself to 50 contacts. Which control from the post-2000 Outlook changes most directly slows that kind of spread?
options: Asking the user before a program reads the address book, and a forced wait before each programmatic send
Encrypting the mailbox at rest
A longer password for Outlook
Disabling spell checking
blocks.explain: Melissa and ILOVEYOU used Outlook's programming interface to collect addresses and send mail. Prompts and delays on those actions break the automatic fan-out.

lessons.title: Code Red, Slammer and Blaster: worms faster than people

blocks.md:
Between 2001 and 2003 three worms showed that unpatched internet-facing services could be taken over faster than any person could respond. All three used **buffer overflows** (the memory bug from *Security from zero*) in Microsoft services for which patches already existed.

**Code Red, July 2001.** Microsoft bulletin MS01-033 (18 June 2001) fixed a buffer overflow in the IIS (Internet Information Services) web server's indexing extension, reported by the security company eEye. CAIDA (the Center for Applied Internet Data Analysis) records that a first version spread from 12 July with a fixed random-number seed, so every copy scanned the same address list. On 19 July a version with a random seed appeared, and more than 359,000 computers were infected in under 14 hours, peaking at more than 2,000 new hosts a minute. CAIDA notes the name came from eEye's analysts, who were drinking Code Red Mountain Dew while working through the night, and because the worm defaced pages with "Hacked by Chinese".

**Slammer (also called Sapphire), 25 January 2003.** David Moore and colleagues' paper *Inside the Slammer Worm* and their CAIDA report on its spread call it the fastest worm in history: it doubled the infected population about every 8.5 seconds, infected more than 90 percent of vulnerable hosts within 10 minutes and reached at least 75,000 hosts. Its 376 bytes of code fitted in a single 404-byte UDP packet (UDP, the User Datagram Protocol, sends packets with no handshake), aimed at Microsoft SQL Server's resolution service on UDP port 1434. Because one packet was enough, each infected machine sent as fast as its network allowed, over 55 million scans per second in total after about three minutes.

It carried no destructive payload, yet the paper reports cancelled airline flights, ATM failures and disrupted 911 emergency terminals, just from network overload. Microsoft had published the fix, bulletin [MS02-039](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security-updates/securitybulletins/2002/ms02-039), on 24 July 2002, six months earlier, and advised blocking port 1434 at firewalls.

blocks.title: Infected hosts over time for a given doubling time (simplified)

scenes.caption: Slammer-like doubling every 8.5 s: the curve saturates within a few minutes. A person reading an alert would arrive after the network was already full.
Blaster-like doubling of about 9 minutes (from Bailey and colleagues' Blaster study): roughly two and a half hours to saturate, still faster than most change processes.

Code Red's doubling of about 37 minutes (Moore and colleagues' Slammer paper): within one hour the infected count is still small. Slower worms leave a window for blocking and patching. Simplified: real worms slow as bandwidth fills.

blocks.code:
import math

def minutes_to_reach(hosts, doubling_seconds):
    # pure doubling from one host, ignoring saturation (simplified)
    doublings = math.log2(hosts)
    return doublings, doublings * doubling_seconds / 60

for name, hosts, dbl in [("Code Red v2", 359_000, 37 * 60),
                         ("Slammer", 75_000, 8.5)]:
    d, m = minutes_to_reach(hosts, dbl)
    print(f"{name:12} {d:4.1f} doublings  {m:6.1f} minutes")

# Output:
# Code Red v2  18.5 doublings   682.8 minutes
# Slammer      16.2 doublings     2.3 minutes
blocks.caption: Real output. Pure doubling gives Code Red about 11.4 hours to 359,000 hosts, close to CAIDA's 'less than 14 hours', and Slammer about 2.3 minutes to 75,000. The model ignores saturation and network limits.

blocks.md: **Blaster, August 2003.** Microsoft bulletin [MS03-026](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security-updates/securitybulletins/2003/ms03-026), first posted on 16 July 2003, fixed a buffer overflow in the Windows RPC (Remote Procedure Call) interface on TCP port 135. Bailey, Cooke, Jahanian and Watson's study *The Blaster Worm: Then and Now* reports a doubling time of about nine minutes early on, at least 100,000 infected Windows systems, and that Microsoft reported that its removal tool cleaned 8 million infected computers in January 2004, months after the patch.

**What changed.**
- On 15 January 2002, after Code Red and other outbreaks, Bill Gates emailed every Microsoft employee making **Trustworthy Computing** the company's highest priority: "when we face a choice between adding features and resolving security issues, we need to choose security."
- **Secure by default.** In Windows XP Service Pack 2 (2004), [Microsoft's documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-xp/bb457029%28v=technet.10%29) says Windows Firewall was enabled by default on all network connections; in earlier XP versions the built-in firewall was off unless a wizard turned it on.

"We patch monthly" did not save anyone from Slammer: the patch was six months old. What matters is whether the patch is actually installed on every exposed system, and whether services that need not face the internet (SQL Server's port 1434, Windows RPC) are reachable at all.

At internet speed, the defence has to be in place before the worm arrives: patches installed, unneeded services unreachable, firewalls on by default, and automatic updates for machines without an administrator. Human response time is measured in minutes; Slammer finished in about ten.

blocks.question: Why did Slammer spread roughly 250 times faster than Code Red?
options: It used a more severe vulnerability
It targeted more popular software
One UDP packet was enough to infect, so each machine sent packets as fast as its bandwidth allowed instead of waiting for TCP handshakes
It exploited weak passwords
blocks.explain: The paper explains Slammer's scanner was limited only by bandwidth because a single UDP packet carried the whole worm. TCP-based worms like Code Red spend time waiting for each connection to be set up.

blocks.question: Slammer's patch had been available for six months. Which change most directly stops a repeat of that situation for home PCs, which have no administrator?
options: Publishing bulletins more often
Automatic updates and a firewall that is on by default
Teaching users to read bulletins
Larger hard drives
blocks.explain: Home users rarely read bulletins. Defaults that install fixes and block unsolicited inbound connections protect people who never configure anything, which is why XP SP2 turned the firewall on.

lessons.title: Conficker: the botnet that made the industry organise

blocks.md: A **botnet** ([NIST](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/botnet): from *robot* and *network*) is a set of infected computers that one controller can command remotely. To receive commands, infected machines must find their controller, and defenders can cut that link by taking the controller's address away.

**Conficker, from November 2008.** Microsoft released bulletin [MS08-067](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security-updates/securitybulletins/2008/ms08-067) on 23 October 2008 for a critical bug in the Windows Server service that allowed remote code execution through a crafted RPC request. [SRI International's analysis](https://www.csl.sri.com/users/vinod/papers/Conficker/) records that Conficker began using it to scan and infect in mid-November, about a month later. Variant B, from late December, added copying itself to USB drives with an `autorun.inf` file (so it ran when a drive was inserted) and guessing passwords on network shares from a list of over 240 common passwords. SRI counted more than 4.7 million IP addresses affected by variant A and 6.7 million by B. The Conficker Working Group's report says nearly everyone places the peak above five million machines.

**Why it was hard to stop.** Instead of a few fixed control addresses, Conficker used a **domain generation algorithm** (DGA): every day each infected PC computed a list of pseudo-random domain names from the date and tried them for updates. The attacker only needed to register one name on the list; defenders had to block or register all of them. The Working Group's report gives the numbers: early versions generated 250 domains a day across eight top-level domains (TLDs, the last part of a name such as `.com` or `.cn`). From 1 April 2009 variant C generated 50,000 a day across more than 100 TLDs, and tried 500 of them.

blocks.title: Domains defenders had to cover each day

scenes.caption: Variants A and B: 250 domains a day over eight TLDs. Registering them all ahead of the attacker was already, in the report's words, an unprecedented effort.
Variant C, from 1 April 2009: 50,000 a day across more than 100 TLDs, including many country registries that had never worked together.
Each C machine tried only 500 of the 50,000, but defenders could not know which 500, so all had to be covered. The attacker's cost stayed at one registration.

blocks.md:
**What the defenders built.** The **Conficker Working Group** (CWG) was an informal coalition of Microsoft, ICANN (the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, which coordinates domain names), domain registries, antivirus vendors and academic researchers. They pre-registered or blocked the generated domains so infected machines could not reach their controller. ICANN told the report's authors it was the first time it had been asked to waive registration fees for security reasons, and it later created a formal process for registries facing such threats.

The report is candid about the outcome: the group saw its biggest failure as the inability to clean infected computers, and millions of A and B infections remained when it was written.

blocks.code:
import math
from collections import Counter

def entropy(label):
    # Shannon entropy in bits per character of the first DNS label
    counts = Counter(label)
    return -sum(c / len(label) * math.log2(c / len(label)) for c in counts.values())

# DNS queries seen by a resolver; the odd ones are made-up examples
queries = ["mail.google.com", "intranet.example.org", "wikipedia.org",
           "qxkvhzwptb.ws", "jzbmyrcxlq.cn", "microsoft.com"]
for q in queries:
    label = q.split(".")[0]
    h = entropy(label)
    flag = "  <- review" if h > 3.0 and len(label) >= 8 else ""
    print(f"{q:22} {h:4.2f}{flag}")

# Output:
# mail.google.com        2.00
# intranet.example.org   2.50
# wikipedia.org          2.64
# qxkvhzwptb.ws          3.32  <- review
# jzbmyrcxlq.cn          3.32  <- review
# microsoft.com          2.95
blocks.caption: Real output. A defender's first look for DGA traffic: random-looking names have higher character entropy. It is only a hint (many legitimate names look random and some DGAs use dictionary words), so in practice it is combined with failed lookups and threat intelligence.

blocks.md: **What changed.** Beyond the coordination model, Conficker hastened the end of a default. [Computerworld reported in June 2011](https://www.computerworld.com/article/1440578/windows-xp-vista-autorun-update-reduces-malware-infections-by-82-2.html) that Microsoft had offered an update in February 2011, later delivered automatically, that stopped USB drives on Windows XP and Vista from offering to run programs when inserted (Windows 7 already behaved this way). Microsoft's own figures, quoted there, showed infections by AutoRun-abusing malware falling by 62 percent on XP SP3 and 82 percent on Vista SP2 since January 2011.

Conficker showed both sides of collective defence: an industry coalition could deny a botnet its control channel at internet scale, but cleaning millions of unmanaged PCs was beyond it. Patching (MS08-067 was a month old) and removing risky defaults (AutoRun) would have prevented most infections.

blocks.question: Why did a DGA make Conficker expensive to fight?
options: It encrypted the domain names
It used IP addresses instead of names
It changed the Windows registry
Defenders had to block or register every generated name each day, while the attacker needed to register only one
blocks.explain: The asymmetry is the point: 50,000 names a day for defenders against one registration for the attacker. Which 500 a given machine tried was unpredictable, so partial coverage was not enough.

blocks.question: The Working Group called which outcome its biggest failure?
options: Being unable to remediate (clean) infected computers, so millions of infections remained
Missing the 1 April 2009 deadline
Failing to get ICANN involved
Failing to identify that MS08-067 was the bug
blocks.explain: The domain blocking largely worked, including for variant C, and ICANN did take part. But blocking the control channel left the infections in place on millions of machines.

lessons.title: 2010: Operation Aurora and Stuxnet bring state operations into view

blocks.md:
Until 2010 most public incidents were worms, viruses and criminals. Two disclosures that year made **state-sponsored operations** (attacks run or backed by a government's intelligence or military services) a public, named reality.

**Operation Aurora.** On 12 January 2010 Google's chief legal officer, David Drummond, wrote on Google's official blog that in mid-December Google had detected a highly sophisticated and targeted attack on its corporate infrastructure originating from China that resulted in the theft of intellectual property. At least twenty other large companies in the internet, finance, technology, media and chemical sectors had been similarly targeted. A primary goal appeared to be the Gmail accounts of Chinese human rights activists; Google believed only two accounts were accessed, and only account information and subject lines.

**Why it worked.** [Wired's Kim Zetter reported](https://www.wired.com/2010/01/operation-aurora/) that the attackers used a previously unknown hole in Internet Explorer: employees visited a malicious website and their browsers were exploited to install malware silently. Microsoft fixed it in bulletin [MS10-002](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security-updates/securitybulletins/2010/ms10-002) (21 January 2010, CVE-2010-0249) and thanked Google, Adobe, McAfee and others for details of limited, targeted attacks. The antivirus company McAfee named the campaign **Operation Aurora** because the malware referred to a file folder named "Aurora" on an attacker's computer. Wired reported that at least 34 companies were said to have been targeted, with source code a major aim.

The structural lesson was about the network. Once one employee's laptop was compromised, it sat **inside** the corporate network, which trusted it. That is pattern 4, the trusted perimeter.

blocks.title: Perimeter trust versus checking every request

scenes.caption: A malicious page exploits the browser on an employee laptop that is already inside the firewall.
Perimeter model: being inside the network is the credential. The compromised laptop reaches the source code server directly.
After Aurora, Google's BeyondCorp design removed the privileged intranet: every request goes through an access proxy that checks the user and the device's state.
A device flagged as unhealthy is refused even with a valid login. The attacker must now defeat the device check too, and every request is logged.

blocks.code:
# Who may open the source-code server? Request data is made up.
def perimeter(req):
    return req["network"] == "corporate"          # inside = trusted

def per_request(req):
    return (req["user_ok"]                          # strong login, right role
            and req["device_managed"]               # known, patched device
            and req["device_healthy"])              # no alert on this device

requests = [
    {"who": "engineer, managed laptop", "network": "corporate",
     "user_ok": True, "device_managed": True, "device_healthy": True},
    {"who": "phished laptop, malware", "network": "corporate",
     "user_ok": True, "device_managed": True, "device_healthy": False},
    {"who": "engineer at home", "network": "internet",
     "user_ok": True, "device_managed": True, "device_healthy": True},
]
for r in requests:
    print(f"{r['who']:26} perimeter={perimeter(r)!s:5} per-request={per_request(r)}")

# Output:
# engineer, managed laptop   perimeter=True  per-request=True
# phished laptop, malware    perimeter=True  per-request=False
# engineer at home           perimeter=False per-request=True
blocks.caption: Real output. The perimeter rule lets the compromised laptop in and keeps the honest engineer at home out; the per-request rule gets both right, because it checks the user and the device on every request rather than the network location.

blocks.md: **What changed after Aurora.** Google went public and named the attack's origin. Google Cloud later wrote that, [in the aftermath of Aurora](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/public-sector/accelerating-governments-zero-trust-journey), it decided remote access through VPNs was not sustainable and began BeyondCorp. The 2014 paper *BeyondCorp: A New Approach to Enterprise Security* (Rory Ward and Betsy Beyer, USENIX ;login:) describes removing the requirement for a privileged intranet and moving corporate applications to the internet behind per-request checks. This became the template for **zero trust** architecture (no request is trusted because of where on the network it comes from; each is checked for user and device), taught in depth in the course *Security architecture and zero trust*.

**Stuxnet.** On 17 June 2010 the antivirus company VirusBlokAda reported new malware that spread using a flaw in how Windows handles shortcut (.lnk) files, for example on USB drives. The security company Symantec's *W32.Stuxnet Dossier* explains its final goal: to reprogram industrial control systems by modifying code on programmable logic controllers (PLCs, the small computers that run machinery), and to hide those changes from the operators. It used several previously unknown Windows vulnerabilities, carried drivers signed with a valid certificate belonging to Realtek Semiconductor, and by late September 2010 about 100,000 hosts were infected, roughly 60 percent of them in Iran.

Ralph Langner, an industrial control system security researcher, later tied Stuxnet's payload to the uranium enrichment centrifuges at Natanz, Iran. The course *Industrial control system and OT security* walks through its controller code and how it replayed normal sensor readings to operators. For this history, three consequences matter:

- **Cyber operations could cause physical damage**, not just steal data.
- **Air gaps are not a guarantee**: in Symantec's likely scenario, the last hop to the isolated programming computers was a USB drive carried by a person.
- **Industrial security became its own field**, with its own standards and teams.

"It came from a nation state, so nothing could have stopped it" is a common excuse. Aurora still needed an unpatched browser and a flat internal network; Stuxnet most likely relied on removable media to reach isolated engineering computers. Sophisticated attackers raise the bar for detection, but basic controls still remove paths.

Aurora showed that a perimeter fails the moment one inside device is compromised, which led to per-request, device-aware access (zero trust). Stuxnet showed that code can break machines and that isolated networks are reached by people carrying media.

blocks.question: In the perimeter model, why did one compromised laptop matter so much?
options: Laptops have more storage than servers
Being inside the corporate network was treated as proof of trust, so the laptop could reach internal systems such as source code servers
The firewall forwarded all traffic to attackers
Browsers store every password in plain text
blocks.explain: The perimeter model checks where a request comes from, not who and what is making it. Once the attacker controlled an inside device, internal services accepted it. Per-request user and device checks close that gap.

blocks.question: Which statement about Stuxnet is supported by Symantec's dossier?
options: It mainly stole credit card data
It was found in 2015
Its goal was to reprogram PLCs and hide the changes from operators
It only spread through email attachments
blocks.explain: The dossier states the final goal was reprogramming industrial control systems by modifying PLC code and hiding the changes. It spread largely by USB and local networks and was reported in June 2010.

lessons.title: Target, Sony and OPM: breaches that reached boardrooms and governments

blocks.md:
Between 2013 and 2015 three breaches showed the scale and kinds of harm an intrusion could cause: stolen payment data, a destroyed corporate network, and the personal secrets of millions of government employees.

**Target, 2013.** The US Senate Commerce Committee's staff report *A "Kill Chain" Analysis of the 2013 Target Data Breach* records that Target confirmed on 19 December 2013 that some 40 million credit and debit card accounts were exposed, for cards used in its US stores between 27 November and 18 December, and on 10 January 2014 that personal information for up to 70 million customers was also stolen. The attackers reportedly entered with credentials stolen from Fazio Mechanical Services, a heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) contractor that had remote access to Target's network for billing and contracts, then installed malware on point-of-sale (POS, the checkout terminals) systems.

**Why it worked.** The report lists missed chances: a vendor with weak security had network access; the network let attackers move from vendor-facing systems to the payment terminals; and Target's FireEye intrusion-detection system raised urgent alerts when the malware was installed, but the security team, according to a Bloomberg Businessweek report cited by the Senate staff, did not act on them. The course *Network attacks and defences* covers the segmentation side in depth.

**Sony Pictures, November 2014.** An FBI agent's 2018 criminal complaint against Park Jin Hyok, a North Korean programmer, describes how on 24 November 2014 Sony Pictures Entertainment employees saw a "Hacked By #GOP" screen (GOP stood for "Guardians of Peace"). The complaint notes the group also targeted people associated with the release of Sony's film *The Interview*. Malware sent to employees (spear phishing: phishing aimed at specific people) had given access; the attackers stole films and confidential data, and a **wiper** (malware meant to destroy data rather than steal it) "effectively rendered thousands of computers inoperable". The complaint ties the same group, which private researchers call the Lazarus Group, to the 2016 USD 81 million Bangladesh Bank theft and to WannaCry.

blocks.title: Records taken (millions), from reports cited in this lesson

scenes.caption: Target: 40 million payment cards and up to 70 million customer records (Senate Commerce staff report).
OPM: 21.5 million people in background-investigation records (OPM, via NPR) and 4.2 million personnel files of current and former employees (Wired).
And about 5.6 million fingerprint images. Unlike a card, a fingerprint or a clearance questionnaire cannot be reissued. Size is not the only measure of harm.

blocks.md: **OPM, 2015.** The US Office of Personnel Management runs background investigations for federal security clearances. Brendan Koerner's account in Wired describes a network engineer noticing on 15 April 2015 a beacon-like signal to a look-alike domain, `opmsecurity.org`, which led to hidden malware. Investigators traced the earliest intrusion to an OPM credential issued to a contractor. The attackers took background-check data, personnel files of 4.2 million people and about 5.6 million fingerprint images. [NPR reported](https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2015/07/09/421502905/opm-21-5-million-social-security-numbers-stolen-from-government-computers) OPM's figure of 21.5 million people affected in the background-investigation databases, including 1.8 million non-applicants, mainly applicants' spouses and cohabitants.

**What changed.**
- **Federal identity.** In June 2015 the White House ran a 30-day **Cybersecurity Sprint** focused on basic hygiene; Wired reports federal use of smartcards for **multi-factor authentication** (MFA: proving identity with something besides a password) rose by more than 70 percent during it.
- **Sanctions as a response.** On 2 January 2015 the [US Treasury announced sanctions](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jl9733) on North Korean government entities under a new executive order, citing the Sony attack.
- **Board-level attention.** Target's breach, explicitly analysed by a Senate committee, made third-party access and alert handling board-level questions.
