import csv, io

# Export of remote-access accounts (made-up rows)
export = """user,type,mfa,last_login_days
a.kim,employee,smartcard,1
b.ross,employee,none,3
vendor-hvac,contractor,none,40
c.diaz,contractor,smartcard,2
svc-backup,service,none,0
"""
for row in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(export)):
    if row["mfa"] != "none":
        continue
    if row["type"] == "service":
        action = "no interactive logins; allow only from backup host"
    elif row["type"] == "contractor":
        action = "HIGH: enforce MFA now; idle " + row["last_login_days"] + " days"
    else:
        action = "enforce MFA"
    print(f"{row['user']:12} {action}")

# Output:
# b.ross       enforce MFA
# vendor-hvac  HIGH: enforce MFA now; idle 40 days
# svc-backup   no interactive logins; allow only from backup host
blocks.caption: Real output, made-up rows. A first audit after Target and OPM: list every remote-access account without MFA. Contractor and vendor accounts come first; service accounts cannot do MFA, so restrict where they can be used instead.

blocks.md: A DHS official told Congress, as [Ars Technica reported](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2015/06/encryption-would-not-have-helped-at-opm-says-dhs-official/), that encryption "would not have helped" at OPM: the attackers had valid credentials, so their queries returned decrypted data. What helps is MFA on every remote login, limiting what each account can read, and acting on alerts. The *Data security* course covers this case.

Target and OPM both began with a third party's credentials and both had warnings that went unanswered. The lasting changes were about identity: MFA for everyone who logs in remotely, tight scoping of vendor access, and an alert process that someone actually owns.

blocks.question: Target's FireEye system alerted when the attackers' data-exfiltration malware was installed. What does the Senate staff report's account say went wrong?
options: The alerts were never generated
FireEye was turned off for the holidays
The alerts fired, but the security team did not act on them
The alerts went to Fazio Mechanical
blocks.explain: The report, citing Bloomberg Businessweek, says urgent alerts triggered with each installation but the team neither reacted nor allowed automatic deletion. Detection without response is the gap.

blocks.question: Why is the OPM fingerprint theft arguably worse than a card theft of similar size?
options: A card can be cancelled and reissued, but a fingerprint and the personal history in a clearance file cannot be changed
Fingerprints are worth more on criminal markets
Fingerprints were stored unencrypted
Card thefts are never reported
blocks.explain: Harm depends on what was taken, not only how many records. Card numbers are replaced routinely; biometrics and clearance histories are permanent and useful to an intelligence service for years.

lessons.title: Leaks: Snowden, the Shadow Brokers and keeping bugs secret

blocks.md:
Two leaks a few years apart changed how people thought about intelligence agencies and software security: one exposed what the US National Security Agency (NSA) collected, the other released the NSA's hacking tools.

**Edward Snowden, 2013.** In June 2013 Edward Snowden, a former NSA contractor, carried out what the US House Intelligence Committee's [2016 review](https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/defenseissues/hpsci_snowden_review_-_unclass_summary_-_final.pdf) calls the largest and most damaging public release of classified information in US intelligence history, removing more than 1.5 million classified documents. The committee found Snowden had obtained colleagues' credentials through misleading means, abused access as a systems administrator, and began unauthorised mass downloading in July 2012. It is mainly an **insider threat** case (harm from someone with legitimate access), covered in depth in the course *Identity governance and privileged access management*.

**What changed for the internet.** In the months after the first publications, the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force, which writes internet protocol standards) discussed pervasive monitoring at its November 2013 plenary, and in May 2014 published [RFC 7258](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7258), *Pervasive Monitoring Is an Attack*: a best current practice stating that such monitoring should be mitigated in the design of IETF protocols where possible. Encrypting traffic by default became an explicit design goal.

**The Shadow Brokers, 2017.** On 14 April 2017 a group calling itself the Shadow Brokers released a set of working exploits that, as [Microsoft's security team wrote in June 2017](https://web.archive.org/web/20221114162711/https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2017/06/16/analysis-of-the-shadow-brokers-release-and-mitigation-with-windows-10-virtualization-based-security/), were soon used to build the wormable malware WannaCry. You studied the result in *Security from zero*: EternalBlue, an exploit for a Windows SMBv1 bug, was public, and Microsoft's fix MS17-010 had been released on 14 March. The script below lays out the dates.

blocks.code:
from datetime import date

patch = date(2017, 3, 14)          # Microsoft MS17-010
events = {"Shadow Brokers leak": date(2017, 4, 14),
          "WannaCry": date(2017, 5, 12),
          "NotPetya": date(2017, 6, 27)}
for name, d in events.items():
    print(f"{name:20} {d}  day {(d - patch).days} after the patch")

# Output:
# Shadow Brokers leak  2017-04-14  day 31 after the patch
# WannaCry             2017-05-12  day 59 after the patch
# NotPetya             2017-06-27  day 105 after the patch
blocks.caption: Real output. Each event found many organisations still unpatched. NotPetya (next lesson) arrived more than three months after the fix.

blocks.title: 2017, in days after Microsoft's MS17-010 patch

scenes.caption: Day 0, 14 March 2017: Microsoft publishes MS17-010, fixing the SMBv1 bugs.
Day 31: the Shadow Brokers publish exploits, including EternalBlue. A patch exists, but now so does free attack code.
Day 59 WannaCry and day 105 NotPetya both spread with EternalBlue among other methods.
Day 246, 15 November 2017: the US government publishes the charter of its Vulnerabilities Equities Process, the rules for deciding whether to tell a vendor about a bug or keep it.

blocks.md:
**The equities question.** When a government agency finds a new vulnerability it faces a trade-off: tell the vendor so everyone is protected, or keep it secret to use for intelligence. The [charter](https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/sites/whitehouse.gov/files/images/External%20-%20Unclassified%20VEP%20Charter%20FINAL.PDF) of the US **Vulnerabilities Equities Process** (VEP), published on 15 November 2017, describes exactly that balance: whether to disseminate the information to the vendor "in the expectation that it will be patched", or temporarily restrict it for national security and law enforcement purposes. Restricted vulnerabilities are reassessed each year.

The leaked tools made the cost of the second choice concrete: a vulnerability kept secret can be stolen, and then everyone running that software is exposed at once.

blocks.prompt: A government team holds an exploit for an unpatched bug in software that hospitals use. Using the 2017 events, what is the risk of keeping it secret that a simple 'only we know about it' argument misses?
blocks.reveal: That it may not stay secret. Tools can be stolen or leaked, as in 2017, and then attackers get a working exploit for software that defenders cannot patch because the vendor was never told. Reporting gives the vendor time to fix it; secrecy bets everyone's safety on the secret holding.

blocks.md: Leaks change risk calculations. Snowden's disclosures pushed internet standards towards encryption by default (RFC 7258). The Shadow Brokers showed that withheld vulnerabilities can escape, which is why governments now publish their rules for disclosure (the VEP charter) and why defenders treat every critical patch as if exploit code will appear soon.

blocks.question: What does the 2017 VEP charter mainly govern?
options: Export controls on encryption software
How CVE numbers are assigned
Bug bounty payments to researchers
Whether the US government discloses a newly found vulnerability to the vendor or temporarily keeps it for intelligence and law enforcement use
blocks.explain: The charter describes balancing equities between dissemination to the vendor (so it gets patched) and temporary restriction for national security purposes, with annual review of restricted items. CVE numbering is run by the CVE Program.

blocks.question: MS17-010 was released on 14 March 2017. Why did WannaCry still find so many victims 59 days later?
options: The patch did not fix EternalBlue
Many organisations had not installed it, and the leak had made a working exploit freely available
WannaCry used a different, unpatched bug
Microsoft withdrew the patch in April
blocks.explain: MS17-010 fixed the bug EternalBlue used. The gap between patch release and installation is where the damage happened, made worse because the leak handed attackers a free, reliable exploit.

lessons.title: NotPetya: a wiper delivered as a software update

blocks.md:
**What happened.** On 27 June 2017 destructive malware spread across Ukraine and then the world. CISA's alert TA17-181A states that its delivery mechanism was M.E.Doc, Ukrainian tax-accounting software: attackers had backdoored M.E.Doc's development environment as early as 14 April 2017, and the malware arrived through the software's update process. Because the code resembled an earlier criminal ransomware called Petya but was a different program, researchers named it **NotPetya**.

It displayed a ransom note, but [analysts at Kaspersky, a Russian antivirus company, concluded](https://securelist.com/expetrpetyanotpetya-is-a-wiper-not-ransomware/78902/) the attackers could not decrypt victims' disks even if paid: it was a **wiper** (malware meant to destroy data) pretending to be ransomware. [ESET's analysis](https://www.welivesecurity.com/2017/06/30/telebots-back-supply-chain-attacks-against-ukraine/) of the same campaign reached the same conclusion about its disk-encryption code.

**Why it spread so far.** CISA lists the methods. The first and, in most cases, most effective was a modified version of **Mimikatz** (a tool that reads Windows login credentials from memory; its author, researcher Benjamin Delpy, released it publicly in May 2011 to show Microsoft the problem, and named it from the French slang *mimi*, cute, so 'cute cats', as [Wired reports](https://www.wired.com/story/how-mimikatz-became-go-to-hacker-tool/)) to steal users' credentials, then use them with standard Windows administration tools (WMIC, the Windows Management Instrumentation Command Line, and PsExec, a Microsoft Sysinternals utility) to run on other machines. It also used the leaked EternalBlue and EternalRomance exploits against unpatched SMBv1. So **patched machines fell too**, whenever a stolen administrator credential worked on them. The courses *Windows for security* and *Privilege escalation and lateral movement* explain why credentials stay in memory and how to limit their reuse.

blocks.title: Why patching alone did not stop NotPetya (toy network)

scenes.caption: The update channel the accounting team trusts delivers the malware to one PC. No vulnerability on the PC was needed.
Exploit only: the leaked SMB exploit works on the unpatched PC and nowhere else. If this were the only method, patching would have contained it.

Exploit plus stolen credentials: an admin password shared across machines opens the patched PC, the file server and the domain controller (the server that runs Windows logins for the whole organisation).
Only lab-pc survives: patched and with its own unique password, it offers neither door. Toy model; the real malware also scanned networks and used other tricks.

blocks.caption: Real output. Same search as the diagram: credentials, not the exploit, decide how far the damage reaches. Unique local administrator passwords (for example set by Microsoft LAPS, the Local Administrator Password Solution) and fewer machines where admins log in shrink the second list.

blocks.md: **What it cost.** Andy Greenberg's account in Wired names victims including the shipping giant Maersk, the drug maker Merck, FedEx's European subsidiary TNT Express, Saint-Gobain, Mondelez and Reckitt Benckiser, and quotes a White House assessment of more than USD 10 billion in total damages. Maersk rebuilt 4,000 servers and 45,000 PCs in about ten days; its recovery depended on one domain controller that happened to survive in an office in Ghana. The course *Incident response and digital forensics* uses Maersk's recovery as a worked example.

**What changed.**
- **Attribution.** On 15 February 2018 the [UK government stated](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/foreign-office-minister-condemns-russia-for-notpetya-attacks) that the Russian military was responsible, saying the attack masqueraded as a criminal enterprise but was principally meant to disrupt, with primary targets in Ukraine's financial, energy and government sectors.
- **Supply-chain thinking.** A trusted update channel was the way in, three years before SolarWinds.
- **Recovery planning.** Maersk's recovery hinged on one domain controller that survived by luck, a lesson for keeping offline, tested copies of identity systems as well as data.

"It looked like ransomware, so paying would have restored our data" was wrong here. Kaspersky showed the attackers could not decrypt the disks. Classify destructive incidents by what the code does, not by what the ransom screen says.

NotPetya combined three patterns: a trusted supplier's update, a known flaw left open (EternalBlue) and reusable administrator credentials. Patching stopped only one of them. Unique credentials, segmentation and offline backups, including of the identity system, decided who recovered.

blocks.question: In the toy network, the domain controller was fully patched. Why was it still taken?
options: Stolen administrator credentials that were valid on it let the malware log in and run normally, with no exploit needed
The patch for MS17-010 did not install correctly
Domain controllers cannot be patched
The update server attacked it directly
blocks.explain: Credential reuse is independent of patching. CISA describes Mimikatz-based credential theft plus WMIC or PsExec as the first and usually most effective method.

blocks.question: NotPetya showed a ransom note. What did Kaspersky's analysis conclude?
options: Paying the ransom always restored files
The malware only encrypted backup files
The attackers could not decrypt victims' disks even after payment, so it behaved as a wiper
It decrypted files after 30 days
blocks.explain: Kaspersky found the installation ID needed for decryption was not usable for recovery, so it was a wiper pretending to be ransomware.

lessons.title: SolarWinds and Log4Shell: what you install and what you import

blocks.md: Lesson 11 showed an update channel used as a weapon against one country. In December 2020 the same idea reached thousands of organisations through a widely used IT product, and a year later a bug in a free logging library reached millions of systems. Both are **supply chain** incidents: the weakness lies in software you obtained from someone else and trusted.

**SolarWinds, 2020.** SolarWinds sells Orion, software that monitors and manages IT networks and therefore runs with wide access inside them. In December 2020 the security company FireEye (its post now lives on [Google Cloud's Mandiant blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/evasive-attacker-leverages-solarwinds-supply-chain-compromises-with-sunburst-backdoor/)) published that it had found a global intrusion campaign gaining access through **trojanised** updates to Orion (a Trojan horse, after the wooden horse of Greek legend, is a program with a useful-looking function that hides a malicious one, as [NIST](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/trojan_horse) defines it). Multiple backdoored updates were **digitally signed** by SolarWinds and posted to its update site from March to May 2020. After a dormant period of up to two weeks, the backdoor, which FireEye named SUNBURST, contacted attacker infrastructure, starting with a DNS lookup of a subdomain of an attacker-controlled domain.

blocks.title: SolarWinds: trust flowing down a signed update (simplified)

scenes.caption: Normal flow: code is built, signed by the vendor and pushed as an update. Customers trust the signature because it proves the update came from the vendor.
The attacker gets into the build process. The backdoor is added before signing, so the signature is valid: it proves origin, not innocence.
Up to about 18,000 customers may have downloaded affected versions between March and June 2020 (SolarWinds' CEO to NPR). After a quiet period, installed copies beacon out.
The attackers chose a small set for hands-on follow-up: the CEO estimated about 100 companies and about a dozen government agencies.

blocks.md: **Response and what changed.** On 13 December 2020 CISA issued [Emergency Directive 21-01](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/ed-21-01-mitigate-solarwinds-orion-code-compromise) ordering US federal agencies to immediately disconnect or power down affected SolarWinds Orion products. On 12 May 2021 [Executive Order 14028](https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2021/05/12/executive-order-on-improving-the-nations-cybersecurity/), *Improving the Nation's Cybersecurity*, required agencies to adopt multi-factor authentication and encryption within 180 days, directed them to plan for **zero trust architecture**, called for guidance under which software suppliers give purchasers a **Software Bill of Materials** (SBOM: a list of the components inside a product), and created a **Cyber Safety Review Board** (CSRB) to review major incidents.

The course *Software supply chain security* covers the build compromise in depth. (The customer estimates in the diagram come from SolarWinds' chief executive, speaking to [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2021/04/16/985439655/a-worst-nightmare-cyberattack-the-untold-story-of-the-solarwinds-hack).)

**Log4Shell, December 2021.** Log4j is a free Java logging library maintained by the Apache Software Foundation (ASF) and built into thousands of applications. The CSRB's first report reconstructs the timeline: on 24 November 2021 a security engineer from Alibaba Cloud reported to the ASF that Log4j's **JNDI lookup** feature (JNDI, the Java Naming and Directory Interface, lets Java look up objects by name, including from remote servers) could be abused; on 9 December the engineer told the ASF that the vulnerability was already being discussed publicly on WeChat, a Chinese messaging platform. The flaw, CVE-2021-44228, let text inside a logged message make Log4j fetch and run code from a remote server: lesson 1's pattern, data treated as control. The course *Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling* covers the mechanism; the [Apache Log4j security page](https://logging.apache.org/log4j/2.x/security.html) lists affected and fixed versions.

The board's conclusion was blunt: Log4j is an "endemic vulnerability", and vulnerable instances will remain in systems "for many years to come, perhaps a decade or longer", largely because organisations could not quickly find every copy.

blocks.caption: Real output, made-up inventory. With an SBOM per application this is a five-minute query; without one, teams spent weeks searching servers. Java 8+ thresholds (Apache security page, CVE records): 2.15.0 for CVE-2021-44228, 2.16.0 for CVE-2021-45046 (2.15.0 was incomplete), 2.17.1 for CVE-2021-44832.

blocks.md: **A board that came and went.** The CSRB published reviews of Log4j, the `Lapsus$` extortion group and a 2023 Microsoft cloud intrusion. In January 2025, [Cybersecurity Dive reported](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/dhs-disbands-advisory-board-csrb/737976/), the acting Homeland Security secretary ended the memberships of all DHS advisory committees, leaving in question the board's investigation of hacks of US telecom companies attributed to a group called Salt Typhoon. Institutions created after incidents last only as long as someone keeps funding and staffing them.

A valid digital signature does not mean software is safe. It proves who published it and that it was not altered afterwards. If the attacker is inside the publisher's build, the malicious code is signed along with everything else, as with SolarWinds.

SolarWinds attacked what you install (a trusted vendor's build), Log4Shell lived in what you import (a free library inside other products). The responses were inventory (SBOMs), verifiable builds, least privilege for powerful tools like network monitors, and review boards that turn incidents into public lessons.

blocks.question: Why did SolarWinds customers' signature checks not catch the backdoor?
options: The attackers stole and used a fake certificate
Customers had turned off signature checks
Orion updates are never signed
The backdoor was inserted during the vendor's own build, before signing, so the update carried SolarWinds' valid signature
blocks.explain: Signatures prove origin and integrity after signing. FireEye found the trojanised updates were digitally signed by SolarWinds because the code was added inside the build process.

blocks.question: Why did the CSRB call Log4j an 'endemic vulnerability'?
options: Because no patch was ever released
Because the library is embedded in so many products that vulnerable copies will persist for years, perhaps a decade or longer
Because it only affected one country
Because Java cannot be updated
blocks.explain: Fixed versions came out within days. The problem was finding and updating every embedded copy across countless products, which is why the board expected vulnerable instances to remain for many years.

lessons.title: MOVEit and xz: mass extortion and the backdoor that almost shipped

blocks.md:
Two recent cases show where the supply chain story went next: a criminal group turning one product's bug into thousands of breaches, and a patient attacker who nearly placed a backdoor in a core piece of Linux.

**MOVEit Transfer, 2023.** MOVEit Transfer, from Progress Software, is a **managed file transfer** product (software companies use to exchange large files with partners). CISA and the FBI's [joint advisory AA23-158A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a) states that, beginning on 27 May 2023, the Cl0p ransomware gang (also tracked as TA505) exploited a previously unknown **SQL injection** vulnerability (CVE-2023-34362), a bug where input is treated as part of a database command: pattern 1 again. Internet-facing MOVEit servers were infected with a web shell named LEMURLOOT, which was used to steal data from the underlying databases.

**Why it mattered.** Cl0p did not encrypt anything. It stole data from many organisations at once and threatened to publish it: **extortion without encryption**. File-transfer servers are attractive because they concentrate sensitive files from many partners in one internet-facing place. [Emsisoft](https://www.emsisoft.com/en/blog/44123/unpacking-the-moveit-breach-statistics-and-analysis/), an antivirus company that tracked public disclosures, counted 2,773 affected organisations and about 95.8 million individuals as of 28 June 2024. The course *Injection: when data becomes code* walks through the bug class and this case.

**The xz-utils backdoor, 2024.** XZ Utils is a compression library and tool found on most Linux systems. Its library, liblzma, was loaded by the OpenSSH server (sshd) on Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora and other Linux distributions that patch sshd to link the systemd library, which in turn links liblzma. So code in liblzma could affect remote logins.

blocks.title: xz-utils: a backdoor years in the making (months from January 2021)

scenes.caption: Late 2021 to 2022: an account named Jia Tan sends useful patches. In 2022 other new accounts pressure the long-time maintainer, Lasse Collin, to move faster and share the work.
March 2023: Jia Tan tags and builds their first release (5.4.2). By then they share maintainership, as the public timeline compiled by software engineer Russ Cox documents.

February and March 2024: releases 5.6.0 and 5.6.1, whose release tarballs (source archives, not the public git tree) contain the backdoor's trigger. Debian unstable and Fedora pre-releases (Rawhide, the Fedora 40 beta) pick them up.
28 and 29 March 2024: Andres Freund investigates slow SSH logins, finds the backdoor and reports it. CISA publishes an alert on 29 March and Debian rolls the package back.

blocks.md: **What happened.** Russ Cox's timeline describes how, over more than two years, the account "Jia Tan" became a diligent contributor and then a maintainer, while other new accounts pressured Lasse Collin about slow progress. Lasse Collin's own [incident page](https://tukaani.org/xz-backdoor/) states the facts plainly: XZ Utils 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 release tarballs contain a backdoor, and they were created and signed by Jia Tan. Cox summarises the effect: the backdoor watched for hidden commands at the start of an SSH session, giving unauthenticated remote code execution to whoever held the attacker's key.

**How it was caught.** [LWN reports](https://lwn.net/Articles/967192/) that software engineer Andres Freund noticed that failed SSH logins were taking a lot of CPU time while micro-benchmarking, and tracked the cause back to liblzma. Cox's timeline records the public disclosure on 29 March 2024. [CISA told users](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2024/03/29/reported-supply-chain-compromise-affecting-xz-utils-data-compression-library-cve-2024-3094) to downgrade to an uncompromised version such as 5.4.6 and to hunt for malicious activity.

blocks.code:
# Check the xz version string a host reports. The two sample strings are
# what `xz --version` prints; the first line names the xz version.
BACKDOORED = {"5.6.0", "5.6.1"}    # CVE-2024-3094 (CISA, 29 March 2024)

def check(version_output):
    first = version_output.splitlines()[0]        # "xz (XZ Utils) 5.6.1"
    version = first.split()[-1]
    if version in BACKDOORED:
        return f"{version}: affected, downgrade or update per your distro"
    return f"{version}: not one of the backdoored releases"

print(check("xz (XZ Utils) 5.6.1\nliblzma 5.6.1"))
print(check("xz (XZ Utils) 5.4.5\nliblzma 5.4.5"))

# Output:
# 5.6.1: affected, downgrade or update per your distro
# 5.4.5: not one of the backdoored releases
blocks.caption: Real output. A fleet check a defender could run on 29 March 2024. `xz --version` prints the xz version at the end of its first line, the format the script parses.

blocks.md: "Open source is safe because many eyes review it" did not hold: the trigger was only in release tarballs, which few people compare against git, and the payload hid in binary test files. It was caught by one engineer chasing a performance anomaly, not by review.

MOVEit showed that one internet-facing product bug can become thousands of data breaches, with no encryption needed for extortion. xz showed a supply chain attack through maintainers themselves. Defences: inventory and fast patching of edge products, and for open source, funding and supporting maintainers, comparing release archives with source, and investigating oddities. The course *Software supply chain security* has two lessons on xz.

blocks.question: Why could reviewers reading the xz git repository miss the backdoor's trigger?
options: The trigger was present in the release tarballs built by Jia Tan, not in the public git tree
The repository was private
Git hides files larger than 1 MB
The code was written in assembly
blocks.explain: Lasse Collin's page says the 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 release tarballs contain the backdoor, created and signed by Jia Tan. Release archives routinely contain generated build files not in git, so a modified one did not stand out.

blocks.question: What made the MOVEit campaign 'extortion without encryption'?
options: Cl0p encrypted files but did not ask for money
MOVEit encrypted the files itself
Victims paid before any data was taken
Cl0p stole data through the SQL injection and web shell and threatened to publish it, without encrypting victims' systems
blocks.explain: The advisory describes data theft through the LEMURLOOT web shell. The leverage was the threat of publication, so backups alone could not help.

lessons.title: What the incidents changed: laws, institutions and safer defaults

blocks.md:
Step back from the individual cases. Most incidents in this course were followed by one or more lasting changes, of four kinds:

- **Law or courts**: convictions that showed a law applied (Morris, Melissa's author), sentences (Mitnick), new laws (the Philippine Electronic Commerce Act after ILOVEYOU), government attribution and sanctions (Sony, NotPetya), executive orders (14028 after SolarWinds).
- **New institutions**: CERT/CC after Morris, the Conficker Working Group, the Cyber Safety Review Board.
- **Safer defaults**: Outlook blocking script attachments, Windows Firewall on by default, AutoRun off for USB drives, Office blocking internet macros, MFA for federal staff.
- **Architecture**: out-of-band signalling after blue boxes, per-request access (BeyondCorp) after Aurora.

blocks.title: Which kind of change followed each incident (this course's reading)

scenes.caption: Each row is an incident, each column a kind of change described in this course. A filled cell means that kind of change followed. This is a teaching summary, not a complete history.
Safer defaults cluster in the mass-internet era (ILOVEYOU to Conficker): vendors learned that most users never change settings, so the default is the security.
Architecture changes are rarest but most durable: separating the control channel (CCIS) and removing network-location trust (BeyondCorp) ended whole classes of attack rather than single techniques.
xz has no filled cell: as told here, the response was patching and debate about supporting maintainers. Not every incident produces a lasting change, which is why near misses deserve study.

blocks.code:
from statistics import median

# (incident, year, change it is tied to in this course, year of change)
pairs = [
    ("Morris worm",    1988, "CERT/CC created",               1988),
    ("ILOVEYOU",       2000, "Philippine E-Commerce Act",     2000),
    ("ILOVEYOU",       2000, "Outlook attachment blocking",   2000),
    ("Code Red",       2001, "Trustworthy Computing memo",    2002),
    ("Blaster",        2003, "XP SP2 firewall on by default", 2004),
    ("Conficker",      2008, "AutoRun off for USB (XP/Vista)", 2011),
    ("Aurora",         2010, "BeyondCorp paper",              2014),
    ("OPM",            2015, "Cybersecurity Sprint",          2015),
    ("Shadow Brokers", 2017, "VEP charter published",         2017),
    ("SolarWinds",     2020, "Executive Order 14028",         2021),
]
lags = [c - i for _, i, _, c in pairs]
print("lags in years:", lags)
print("median lag:", median(lags), "years; longest:", max(lags))

# Output:
# lags in years: [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 3, 4, 0, 0, 1]
# median lag: 0.5 years; longest: 4
blocks.caption: Real output. Years between an incident and the change this course ties to it. Fast responses are usually rules and patches; deeper changes to defaults and architecture (AutoRun, BeyondCorp) take years because they break existing habits and products.

blocks.md:
**Five questions to ask of any new incident.** The patterns from lesson 1 become a checklist you can apply to tomorrow's news:

1. Is some input being treated as an instruction? (blue boxes, Log4Shell, MOVEit)
2. Was a fix available but not installed, or a needless service exposed? (Slammer, Conficker, WannaCry)
3. Was a person persuaded to do something? (Mitnick, ILOVEYOU)
4. Did being inside the network or holding one credential grant too much? (Aurora, Target, OPM, NotPetya)
5. Did it arrive through a supplier, update or dependency? (NotPetya, SolarWinds, xz)

Most incidents answer yes to two or three. Each yes points to a family of defences you have now seen in action.

blocks.prompt: A new incident report says: attackers phoned a company's IT help desk pretending to be an employee, got the employee's multi-factor authentication reset, logged in to a VPN and moved from there to the virtualisation servers. Which of the five questions does it answer yes to?
blocks.reveal: Question 3 (a person persuaded: the help desk, as in Mitnick's era) and question 4 (one credential plus being on the network gave access to critical servers, as at Target and OPM). The defences follow: call-back verification for resets, MFA that resists phishing, and per-request access with segmentation so a VPN login does not reach the hypervisors.

blocks.md: **Practice.** History is learned by reading primary sources. Pick one incident and read its original report end to end: CISA's advisories (for example [AA23-158A on MOVEit](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)), the [CERT/CC history](https://www.sei.cmu.edu/history-of-innovation/fostering-growth-in-professional-cyber-incident-management/) or the CSRB's Log4j review, and write down the four answers this course uses: what happened, why it worked, what it cost, what changed. For hands-on investigation of incidents in a legal lab, [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/) offers free investigation challenges, and [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/) from Carnegie Mellon teaches the fundamentals behind them. Only practise on systems you own or are explicitly allowed to test.

Incidents changed security through four channels: law, institutions, defaults and architecture. Defaults and architecture protect people who never read a bulletin, so they matter most. When you meet a new incident, ask the five questions, then ask which of the four channels should change.

blocks.question: Which kind of change protected the most people who never read a security bulletin?
options: Criminal convictions
New review boards
Safer defaults such as firewalls on by default, blocked script attachments and AutoRun turned off
Government attribution statements
blocks.explain: Convictions and boards matter, but defaults act on every machine automatically. Most home users never configured anything, so turning protections on by default reached them directly.

blocks.question: An attacker gets a vendor's support account, signs in remotely, and reaches payment terminals because the network is flat. Which earlier case does this most resemble, and which defence fits?
options: Slammer; block UDP 1434
Target; MFA and tight scoping for vendor access plus segmentation of payment systems
Melissa; attachment filtering
Stuxnet; USB control
blocks.explain: Target's attackers used an HVAC contractor's credentials and reached point-of-sale systems. Vendor accounts with MFA and only the access they need, plus a segmented payment network, address both steps.
